posts.text:
Wrapping up an inspiring summer at the NQCC!

Our 2025 summer placement students recently wrapped up their projects with some incredible final presentations – and the breadth of their work was nothing short of outstanding. From developing new tools and control systems in ion trapping to advancing superconducting qubit research, building systems for neutral atom experiments, and even supporting the NQCC's annual flagship event – the UK Quantum Hackathon 2025 – their contributions have been truly remarkable.

Ion Trapping Quantum Computing:
- Ian Alaman built a Python package for generating energy level and pulse sequence diagrams.
- Zoe Smith connected the Ion Trapping lab’s devices to a real-time monitoring dashboard.
- Muhammad Masood (our first Master’s student) completed his MSc thesis in Applied Quantum Computing while developing a modular laser distribution and control system.

Superconducting Quantum Computing:
- Lily Shen investigated the detection and mitigation of TLS losses in superconducting resonators and qubits.
- Daniel Hesk developed workflows to fine-tune quantum device amplifiers for optimal qubit signal readings.

Neutral Atom Quantum Computing:
- Myles Harrison created systems supporting the production of a 3D Magneto-optical Trap.
- Navaneeth Hari Krishnan designed and built architecture for PDH locking - instrumental in enabling two-qubit entanglement gates.

Quantum Computing Innovation: 
- Oscar Ryley coordinated logistics and on-site support for the UK Quantum Hackathon 2025, among other events.

A huge thank you to all the supervisors and mentors who supported these projects, and a big well done to our students for their hard work, creativity, and commitment to advancing quantum technologies. We wish each of them the very best in their next steps, and look forward to seeing the impact they’ll make on the future of quantum computing!

#QuantumComputing #CareersInQuantum #SummerPlacements #STEMCareers #FutureOfQuantum

UK Research and Innovation EPSRC STFC Quantum Software Lab

💡Quantum Computing for Energy Workshop💡

I facilitated for the NQCC's workshop, bridging the gap between Quantum Computing research and the Energy Sector, at The Royal Society; in partnership with the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.

The day's insightful discussion explored how advancements in Quantum Computing could create new opportunities across the energy ecosystem. A range of speakers from across government, academia, and industry provided their perspectives, with a focus on collaboration, practically adopting technologies, and enabling research into real-world use cases.

I handled event logistics, timings, and had the chance to facilitate two breakout sessions. Whilst managing these aspects, I had the opportunity to learn from a variety of experts and reflect on how pivotal end-users are in defining how a technology develops.

A highlight was seeing my branding on screens and banners in the historic hall at the Royal Society, with attendees commenting on the contrast of discussing the future of energy in such a storied, ancient building.

This was another of the many responsibilities I was given during my Summer Placement at the National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC). I want to extend a huge thank you to Mariana Manso for giving me the opportunity to work on this event, and to Rob Whiteman for his support.

posts.text:
🎮 DurJam: Remastered (2025) 🎮

Sparked by the positive reception to my Godot Tutorial for DurHack 2024, which encouraged a large number of its participants to explore game development for the first time, I decided to create the opportunity for a community that I was looking for.

After a five year hiatus, I organised DurJam, the Durham University Computing Society Game Jam, bringing the event back for the first time since 2020.

Our hybrid event, which took place in June, brought students together to work on collaborative projects, share knowledge through workshops, and laid the groundwork for a supportive group of student game developers.

With a focus on rebuilding (or 'remastering') the community, I undertook projects that created lasting resources for future developers. For example, as the Web Developer and Gaming Editor for The Bubble Durham I joined community members in writing games journalism, publishing our work.

I'm particularly proud of my work producing a series of video workshops. These tutorials were led by members of the Durham tech community: Kaalkidan (Kaal) Sahele, Maks Nowak, Luka Mihajlovic, Eleanor Claxton, Toby O'Donoghue, and myself. Many thanks to everyone who shared their expertise on a range of relevant topics.

These tutorials will help shape a growing game development community at Durham, and beyond, that I am excited to see flourish this upcoming academic year.

posts.text:
Edward Tian built GPTZero, one of the most widely used AI detection tools. He shared his 4 principles for using AI in writing with me. 

GPTZero was acquired by Superhuman in June, and one of Edward and his team's first contributions has been to suggest AI writing principles for the larger company. He talked me through them in my latest newsletter this week. 

1. 𝐀𝐈 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐟𝐭, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐨𝐧𝐞.

2. 𝐄𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠.
Edward says he learned the importance of editing from his creative writing professor at Princeton, John McPhee. 

3. 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐲.
The reader deserves more effort than the time it takes them to read what you sent.

4. 𝐋𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫.
Edward borrowed this from the classic inverted pyramid in journalism. "Prioritize and highlight the most important information, because AI tends to generate more and more, and the critical points get lost in the noise," he says. 

His take on where we are now: "Whether it's a year ago or now, these tools still aren't fully producing great work, great summaries, great notes on their own. You still need good editorial and writing judgment."

I've seen a lot of AI writing and communications policies, and these four succinct points capture a lot. Is there anything missing? 

Link to the full interview in the comments.

Superhuman users have been asking us for a notetaker for a long time. Meeting notes are one of the clearest, most valuable places where AI can help, and it’s a category I’ve spent a lot of time with.

That’s part of what led us to Fathom. And today, I’m excited to share that Fathom.ai is now part of Superhuman.

Richard White and the Fathom team have built an excellent product and a team with deep expertise in this category. What’s especially interesting to me is where meeting notes can go next. The value isn’t only in capturing and summarizing a conversation. It’s in making what was discussed, decided, and committed to useful in the work that follows.

That fits naturally with what we’re building at Superhuman. Fathom adds meeting context to the context already available across email, calendar, docs, and other places people work.

We’re already working together on what comes next, and I believe we have an opportunity to set a new bar for the category. I’m very excited to welcome the Fathom team to Superhuman.
